title: Radiation 101
question: What is radiation oncology and how does treatment actually flow?
html:
Before you get into the technical details of the rotation, it helps to step back and see the big picture: what radiation oncology actually does, and how it fits alongside the other parts of cancer care. Almost everything you'll learn on this Sub-I builds on this framework, so it's worth having it in your back pocket before day one.

Don't worry about memorizing it all at once. You'll see these ideas over and over, and they'll stick fast.

On This Page
  1. The Three Pillars of Cancer Treatment
  2. The Four Treatment Intents
  3. The Radiation Treatment Journey

The Three Pillars of Cancer Treatment

Nearly every cancer patient you meet is treated with some combination of three specialties. Each one brings a different tool to the table:

1
Surgical Oncology

Removes the cancer physically: taking out the primary tumor, sampling or removing lymph nodes, or debulking bulky disease. Surgery is a local therapy: it treats one specific place.

2
Medical Oncology

Treats cancer with drugs that travel through the whole body: chemotherapy, immunotherapy, targeted therapy, hormone therapy. This is systemic therapy, and it matters because cancer cells can be present beyond the visible tumor, even when scans look clean.

3
Radiation Oncology

Treats cancer locally, like surgery, but uses radiation beams or radioactive sources instead of a scalpel. It can reach places that are hard to operate on, and can sometimes treat a cancer when surgery isn't an option.

Because these three specialties often care for the same patient, cancer treatment is a team sport. Plans get worked out together, sometimes at a formal tumor board, and sometimes just through surgeons, medical oncologists, and radiation oncologists talking through a case. When you hear “multidisciplinary,” this is what it means.

The Four Treatment Intents

One of the first bits of vocabulary to pick up is why radiation is being given. You'll hear these four words constantly, in consults, on rounds, and in notes, so getting comfortable with them early pays off.

1
Definitive

Radiation is the main treatment, aiming to cure or permanently control the cancer. Sometimes paired with concurrent chemotherapy.
Example: chemoradiation for locally advanced head and neck cancer in a patient who isn't having surgery.

2
Adjuvant

Given after another main treatment, usually surgery, to lower the chance the cancer comes back. The visible tumor is already gone; radiation cleans up microscopic disease left behind.
Example: whole-breast radiation after a lumpectomy.

3
Neoadjuvant

Given before another treatment, usually surgery, to set that treatment up for success, often by shrinking or downstaging the tumor.
Example: chemoradiation before surgery for rectal cancer.

4
Palliative

Given to relieve symptoms rather than to cure: pain, bleeding, blockage, or pressure on nerves. Usually shorter than definitive treatment.
Example: a short course of radiation to a painful bone metastasis.

Two questions place any case into the right bucket:
1. What's the goal — cure/control, or symptom relief?
2. When is radiation given — before, after, or instead of another local treatment?

The Radiation Treatment Journey

Every radiation patient moves through the same basic pipeline. You'll see each step play out again and again, so use this as your map whenever you're unsure what happens next:

1
Consult
→
2
CT Simulation
→
3
Contouring
→
4
Treatment Planning
↓
5
Plan Review / QA
→
6
Treatment Delivery
→
7
On-Treatment Visits
→
8
Follow-Up
  1. Consult. The team decides whether to treat, what the intent is, and the general approach.
  2. CT Simulation. A planning CT is taken with the patient in the exact position and immobilization they'll be in for treatment.
  3. Contouring. The physician team outlines the targets and the organs at risk (OARs) on that simulation CT.
  4. Treatment Planning. Dosimetry uses those contours to design the beams and dose so the target gets covered while nearby normal tissue is spared.
  5. Plan Review / QA. The physician reviews the plan, and medical physics independently checks that it can be delivered safely and accurately.
  6. Treatment Delivery. The patient is positioned the same way each day and the approved plan is delivered, sometimes a single session, sometimes many over several weeks.
  7. On-Treatment Visits (OTVs). During treatment, patients are seen regularly (often weekly) to check on symptoms, manage side effects, and make sure things are on track.
  8. End of Treatment / Follow-Up. Afterward, the patient is watched for recovery from acute side effects, response of the cancer, recurrence, and any late toxicity.
High-Yield Takeaway If you remember one thing, remember the pipeline: Consult → Simulation → Contouring → Planning → QA → Treatment → OTVs → Follow-Up. Keep that sequence in your head and you'll always know roughly where a patient is in their course, and what's coming next.

title: How Radiation Works
question: Why does radiation actually work, biologically and physically?
html:
You will hear a lot of physics and radiobiology language during a Rad Onc Sub-I: dose, fractionation, α/β ratio, isodose lines, IMRT, VMAT, SBRT, and more. At first it can feel like you're expected to remember an entire physics course before you can understand what's happening.

You are not.

You do not need to master the equations or relearn all of cell biology to succeed on this rotation. You just need a working mental model for three things: what radiation is doing biologically, the vocabulary we use to describe a dose, and the kinds of radiation we have to work with. Once you have those three, the next page, Radiation Modalities, will show you how we actually shape and deliver that radiation to a patient.

Here's the roadmap for this page: Part One — radiobiology, what radiation does to cells and why we split treatment into fractions. Part Two — physics vocabulary, how we measure and describe a dose. Part Three — the building blocks, the particles we use, and a bridge into modalities.

On This Page
  1. Part One: Radiobiology, the Short Version
  2. Part Two: Physics Vocabulary, the Short Version
  3. Part Three: The Building Blocks of a Treatment
  4. Where This Leads: Radiation Modalities

Part One: Radiobiology, the Short Version

How Does Radiation Kill Cancer Cells?

Radiation kills cancer cells primarily by damaging their DNA. The goal is to cause enough DNA damage that the cell can no longer successfully divide. Double-strand breaks, where both strands of the DNA molecule are broken, are particularly difficult for cells to repair accurately. If the damage is unrepaired or misrepaired, the cell may develop lethal chromosomal abnormalities when it attempts to divide, ultimately leading to mitotic catastrophe and cell death.

Direct vs. Indirect Damage

Mechanism 1
Direct Damage

Radiation deposits energy directly in the DNA molecule itself.

Mechanism 2
Indirect Damage

Radiation ionizes water molecules, producing free radicals and reactive oxygen species that then damage DNA.

With the photon radiation used in most external beam treatment, indirect damage is the predominant mechanism. This distinction matters when we get to the oxygen effect below.

Fractionation and the Four R's

Fractionation means dividing the total radiation dose into multiple smaller treatments rather than giving it all at once. Why do we do this? The classic answer is the four R's of radiobiology:

1
Repair

Normal tissues are generally better able to repair sublethal DNA damage between fractions than tumor cells. Fractionation gives normal tissue time to recover while continuing to damage the tumor.

2
Reoxygenation

Hypoxic tumor cells are more resistant to radiation. As treatment shrinks a tumor, previously hypoxic areas may become better oxygenated, and therefore more radiosensitive, during later fractions.

3
Repopulation

Surviving tumor cells can keep dividing during treatment. This is why we avoid unnecessary interruptions, particularly for fast-growing tumors like head and neck squamous cell carcinoma.

4
Redistribution

Cells in G2/M are more radiosensitive; cells in S phase are more resistant. Between fractions, surviving cells cycle, increasing the chance a later fraction catches them in a sensitive phase.

The fifth R — Radiosensitivity. You may also hear about a fifth R, intrinsic radiosensitivity: different tumors and normal tissues have different inherent sensitivities to radiation, which helps explain why some cancers respond to radiation more readily than others.

For rounds, remember: fractionation lets us exploit the differences between tumor and normal tissue, and the four R's explain why.

The α/β Ratio: Why Fraction Size Matters

You'll hear the α/β ratio frequently. You do not need to calculate it on your Sub-I, but you should understand what it means: it describes how sensitive a tissue is to fraction size, how much radiation is given at each treatment.

α/β ≈ 10 Gy
High α/β
  • Most tumors
  • Early-responding tissues (skin, mucosa)
α/β ≈ 1–4 Gy
Low α/β
  • Late-responding normal tissues (spinal cord, connective tissue)
  • Some tumors, most notably prostate cancer

The practical takeaway: low α/β tissues are more sensitive to changes in fraction size. This helps explain why:

  • Larger fractions can increase the risk of late normal-tissue toxicity.
  • Smaller fractions can better protect late-responding tissues.
  • Prostate cancer, with its relatively low α/β, is particularly well suited to hypofractionated and ultra-hypofractionated treatment.
Optional: what are BED and EQD2?▾

BED and EQD2 are tools based on the linear-quadratic model that let us compare different dose and fractionation schedules on a common scale. For your Sub-I, recognize the terms and understand what they're trying to accomplish, you do not need to calculate them unless specifically asked.

The Oxygen Effect

When radiation produces free radicals, oxygen can help “fix” the resulting DNA damage, making it more permanent and harder for the cell to repair. As a result, hypoxic tumor cells are more resistant than well-oxygenated cells. The oxygen enhancement ratio (OER) is roughly 2–3 for low-LET radiation. This helps explain why bulky, poorly vascularized, or necrotic tumors can be harder to control, and why reoxygenation matters during fractionated treatment.

Oxygen is a radiosensitizer. Hypoxia makes tumors more radioresistant.

Part Two: Physics Vocabulary, the Short Version

You'll hear these terms constantly. You do not need the underlying equations, but you should know what they mean.

Dose
Gray (Gy) is the unit of absorbed radiation dose. 1 Gy = 1 joule/kg.
Fraction
One treatment session. For example, 70 Gy in 35 fractions = 2 Gy per fraction.
Conventional Fractionation

Approximately 1.8–2 Gy per fraction.

Hypofractionation

Fewer fractions, with a larger dose per fraction.

Ultra-Hypofractionation

Very few fractions, with a substantially larger dose per fraction.

SBRT / SRS

Highly conformal, high-dose treatment delivered in a small number of fractions.

You'll see these throughout the rotation. For example, 40 Gy in 15 fractions is a common hypofractionated breast regimen.

Part Three: The Building Blocks of a Treatment

Everything above is about what radiation does. The last piece before we talk about how it's delivered is the raw material itself: the particles we treat with. The single most useful question for each one is “where does it deposit its dose?”

1
Photons

The workhorse of external beam RT, produced by a linear accelerator (LINAC). They penetrate deeply and continue past the target, producing an exit dose. This is why deep tumors are treated with multiple beams or arcs that overlap at the target while spreading out dose to normal tissue.

2
Electrons

Useful for superficial targets. They deposit most of their dose over a shallow depth and then fall off quickly, handy for skin cancers, superficial lesions, scar boosts, and some shallow nodal targets.

3
Protons

Little dose along the entrance path, most of their energy released at a defined depth (the Bragg peak), then a sharp falloff. Valuable when a tumor sits next to a critical structure, or in pediatric patients. Assumed relative biological effectiveness (RBE) of about 1.1 versus photons.

Where This Leads: Radiation Modalities

Knowing the particles is only half the story. What turns a beam of photons into a real, deliverable treatment is how we shape, aim, and schedule it, and that's exactly what the next page covers. When you hear terms like IMRT, VMAT, SBRT, SRS, and brachytherapy, those are not new kinds of radiation; they're different ways of delivering the particles you just met, each chosen to put dose on the target while sparing everything around it.

So carry these three questions into the Modalities page, they're the lens an attending uses when looking at any plan:

  1. Where is the target?
  2. What are the nearby organs at risk (OARs)?
  3. How well does the dose conform to the target while sparing normal tissue?
High-Yield Summary
  • Radiation kills cells primarily through DNA damage, especially lethal double-strand breaks. With photons, much of this happens indirectly through free radicals.
  • We fractionate because of the four R's: repair, reoxygenation, repopulation, redistribution (plus a fifth, intrinsic radiosensitivity).
  • The α/β ratio describes how sensitive a tissue is to fraction size; low α/β tissues are the most sensitive to changes in fraction size.
  • Oxygen increases radiosensitivity, and hypoxia makes tumors more resistant.
  • Gy measures absorbed dose, and a fraction is one treatment session.
  • Photons are the workhorse of external beam RT, electrons suit superficial targets, and protons can reduce dose beyond the target.

title: Radiation Modalities
question: What machines and techniques are we actually treating with?
html:
On a Rad Onc Sub-I you'll hear LINAC, VMAT, CBCT, SRS, and SBRT in almost every conversation. You don't need to be an expert in any of them. You need to be conversationally fluent, and the fastest way to get there is to learn each technique by the one thing that makes it different from its neighbor.

For every technique, ask: what can this do that the one before it can't?
On This Page
  1. The Big Split: External Beam vs. Brachytherapy
  2. The LINAC and the MLC
  3. Shaping the Dose: 3D-CRT → IMRT → VMAT
  4. IGRT: Aiming Every Day
  5. Stereotactic: SRS vs. SBRT
  6. Brachytherapy: LDR vs. HDR
  7. Cheat Sheet

The Big Split: External Beam vs. Brachytherapy

Every modality falls on one side of a single question: where is the radiation source?

Source outside
External Beam (EBRT)

A machine outside the patient aims radiation at the target. This is most of what you'll see on your Sub-I.

Source inside
Brachytherapy

A radioactive source is placed inside or right next to the tumor. Dose falls off steeply with distance, so the tumor gets a very high dose while nearby tissue is spared.

External beam brings the radiation to the patient. Brachytherapy brings the source to the tumor.

The LINAC and the MLC

The linear accelerator (LINAC) is the workhorse of radiation oncology. It accelerates electrons to produce high-energy X-rays (photons), and it can also send out the electron beam itself for superficial targets like skin. In the vault it looks like a big rotating arm, the gantry, swinging around a patient lying on the couch.

Inside the head of the gantry is the multileaf collimator (MLC): dozens of thin, computer-controlled metal leaves that slide in and out to shape the beam to the target and block normal tissue. Almost every technique below is really just a different way of using the MLC.

Shaping the Dose: 3D-CRT → IMRT → VMAT

Think of these as three rungs on a ladder. Each rung keeps everything from the one below and adds one new trick.

1
3D-CRT
Baseline

A few fixed beams, each shaped to the outline of the target. The dose is uniform across each beam.

Classic use: simple targets and palliative treatment, like a painful bone metastasis, where fast and simple wins.

2
IMRT
+ Intensity modulation

Still fixed beam angles, but the MLC varies the intensity within each beam, so dose can wrap around the target and carve away from nearby organs.

Classic use: head and neck cancer, where the target hugs the spinal cord and parotid glands.

3
VMAT
+ Rotating gantry

IMRT delivered while the gantry rotates around the patient, with the MLC reshaping the beam continuously along the arc.

Classic use: the same situations as IMRT. It's now one of the most common techniques you'll see.

IMRT + a rotating gantry = VMAT.

IGRT: Aiming Every Day

A beautiful plan is useless if the patient isn't lying where the plan expects. Image-guided radiation therapy (IGRT) means imaging the patient on the treatment machine right before each treatment and shifting them into position.

The version you'll see most is cone-beam CT (CBCT): a quick 3D X-ray taken on the LINAC and overlaid on the planning CT. For prostate, you may also hear about fiducial markers, tiny implanted seeds that show up clearly on imaging.

The rule of thumb: the tighter the dose, the more IGRT matters. That's why it's essential for the stereotactic treatments below.

IGRT answers one question: “Is the patient where we expected them to be today?”

Stereotactic: SRS vs. SBRT

Stereotactic treatment means very high doses, in very few fractions (usually 1–5), with very small margins. The only difference between the two names is where in the body the target is.

Brain
SRS · Stereotactic Radiosurgery

Stereotactic radiation to targets inside the skull. Despite the name, there is no scalpel.

Classic use: brain metastases, vestibular schwannomas, meningiomas, AVMs, trigeminal neuralgia.

Body
SBRT / SABR

The same approach applied to targets outside the brain.

Classic use: early-stage lung cancer, and small tumors or oligometastases in the liver, spine, adrenal gland, or bone.

Why the obsession with setup? Stereotactic plans use tiny margins and a steep dose falloff, so being off by a few millimeters could miss the tumor or overdose a neighboring organ. That's why these patients get extra-careful immobilization and image guidance.

You may hear different platforms named (Gamma Knife, CyberKnife, LINAC-based SRS). You don't need to know the differences, just that they're all ways to deliver stereotactic radiation.

SRS = stereotactic to the brain. SBRT = stereotactic to the body.

Brachytherapy: LDR vs. HDR

Brachytherapy is a procedure, not a trip to the vault. An applicator or catheter is placed in or near the tumor (often under anesthesia or sedation), imaging is done, and the dose is planned around the applicator. The two flavors differ in how fast the dose is delivered.

Low dose rate · long time
LDR

Radiation is delivered slowly over a long period.

Classic use: permanent radioactive seed implants for prostate cancer.

High dose rate · short time
HDR

A high-activity source is temporarily sent through the applicator or catheter for a few minutes, then removed.

Classic use: cervical, endometrial, and some prostate and breast treatments.

Pearl: Cervical Cancer

For definitive treatment of cervical cancer, brachytherapy is essential. It is combined with external beam and cannot be replaced by simply giving more external beam, because nothing else gets such a high dose onto the cervix while sparing the bladder and rectum.

Cheat Sheet

TechniqueWhat sets it apartThink of it for
LINACThe main machine: makes photons (and electrons)Nearly all external beam
MLCMetal leaves that shape the beamEvery modern plan
3D-CRTFixed beams, uniform intensitySimple targets, palliation
IMRTIntensity varies within each beamTargets next to critical organs (head and neck)
VMATIMRT while the gantry rotatesSame as IMRT, very common
IGRT / CBCTImaging before each treatment to check positionEverything, and it's critical for stereotactic
SRSStereotactic, brainBrain mets, benign brain tumors
SBRTStereotactic, bodyEarly lung cancer, oligometastases
LDR brachyLow dose rate, long time (permanent seeds)Prostate seeds
HDR brachyHigh dose rate, short time (temporary source)Cervix, endometrium

title: How to Give a Presentation
question: How do I present new patients, follow-ups, and OTVs effectively?
html:
On most Rad Onc Sub-Is, you will not be expected to present polished patients on your first day. Usually you start out shadowing: watching how the team runs consults, follow-ups, and on-treatment visits, and getting a feel for the flow of clinic. As you gain comfort, you can ask to do more, and one of the best things to ask for is the chance to present patients yourself.

That's worth doing, and the good news is that presenting is one of the more learnable parts of a Rad Onc Sub-I. Unlike a lot of the rotation, it has a predictable structure, so with a framework in hand it gets more comfortable quickly.

1
New Patient Consult

The longest presentation. Tell the patient's story from diagnosis to the clinical question facing radiation oncology today.

2
Follow-Up

What has happened since the last visit: treatment, response, toxicity, and next steps.

3
On-Treatment Visit

Short and repetitive. How the patient is tolerating treatment, right now.

This page focuses on the spoken presentation and the reasoning behind it. It assumes you've already done the chart review described in “The Rad Onc Consult”: reading the medical oncology and surgical oncology notes, reviewing the pathology and imaging yourself, and looking up the relevant guideline. Your job now is to turn that preparation into a clear, concise presentation with your own clinical reasoning.

On This Page
  1. The One Rule That Matters Most
  2. The New Patient Presentation
  3. The Follow-Up Presentation
  4. The OTV Presentation

The One Rule That Matters Most

Do not just relay the chart.

It's easy to repeat the referring note, including its staging and treatment recommendation, without doing your own thinking. Resist this. Look at the imaging yourself, work out the stage yourself, and form your own opinion about the treatment before you present. You will sometimes be wrong. That's expected. The point is to show that you engaged with the case and can explain your reasoning, not that you arrived at the exact answer.

Sounds Like “I'd stage her as T1c N0, and my thought was whole-breast radiation, although I wasn't sure whether she'd also be a candidate for partial-breast irradiation.”

That's much more valuable than simply repeating the referral's recommendation.

The New Patient Presentation

Your goal is to tell the patient's story from diagnosis to the clinical question being asked of radiation oncology today.

The Skeleton

  1. One-liner
  2. Oncologic history, chronologically
  3. Imaging, focusing on what you saw
  4. Pathology, including histology, grade, and biomarkers
  5. Stage, using your own TNM and group stage
  6. Relevant PMH and treatment history
  7. Assessment
  8. Plan, including your proposed approach and the actual recommendation

1. Build a Strong One-Liner

The one-liner should orient the room in a single sentence. A strong one generally includes: age and sex; relevant menopausal or performance status, when it affects management; diagnosis, including site, histology, and key biomarkers; where they are in their treatment course; and the reason for consultation.

Sounds Like “This is Ms. R, a 58-year-old postmenopausal woman with newly diagnosed, node-negative, ER/PR-positive, HER2-negative invasive ductal carcinoma of the left breast, status post breast-conserving surgery, referred for consideration of adjuvant radiation.”

That single sentence conveys the disease, biology, treatment history, and clinical question before you've said a second sentence.

2. Tell the Oncologic History Chronologically

Think of the oncologic history as a timeline, not a paragraph. The listener should follow the story forward without jumping backward in time. Include: presentation, diagnostic workup, pathology, definitive or primary treatment, systemic therapy, prior radiation (always look for it, since it can significantly affect treatment options), and current status.

3. Review the Imaging Yourself

Do not simply read the radiology report. Look at the actual images yourself and know what you're looking at. You should be able to identify the primary lesion, relevant nodes, metastatic disease, and other findings that affect the plan. When you present, focus on what matters for radiation rather than listing every finding.

4. Know the Pathology

Pull out the features that actually affect management: histology, grade, receptor or biomarker status, margins, lymphovascular or perineural invasion when relevant, nodal involvement, and molecular or disease-specific markers. You should be able to explain why each important feature matters to the treatment plan.

5. Stage the Patient Yourself

Before you present, determine the patient's clinical and/or pathologic TNM stage and group stage. Do not simply copy the stage from another note; if you've worked through the imaging, pathology, and operative report yourself, you should be able to explain how you got there.

6. Build the Assessment

The assessment is where you synthesize the case rather than repeat it. In one or two sentences, state: age and clinical status, diagnosis (histology, grade, biomarkers), stage, treatment already received, and the specific clinical decision facing the team.

Sounds Like “Ms. R is a 58-year-old postmenopausal woman with pT1c pN0, Stage IA, grade 2, ER/PR-positive, HER2-negative invasive ductal carcinoma of the left breast, status post breast-conserving surgery with negative margins, now presenting for consideration of adjuvant radiation to reduce her risk of local recurrence.”

7. Make a Guideline-Anchored Plan

This is where a strong Sub-I can really stand out. Your plan should answer four questions:

  1. What is the intent?
  2. What radiation are you recommending?
  3. How would you deliver it?
  4. What decisions are still open?

Whenever possible, know the guideline and the key trial behind your recommendation. You're not expected to know every detail or always be correct, you're expected to show that your recommendation comes from somewhere.

Worked Example: Ms. R's Plan
Intent

Adjuvant, to reduce local recurrence after breast-conserving surgery.

Recommendation

Per NCCN, she is a candidate for whole-breast radiation or accelerated partial-breast irradiation. Radiation omission is an option for select older patients with favorable, hormone-receptor-positive, node-negative disease, but at age 58 she does not meet those criteria.

Dose and Technique

Moderate hypofractionation, approximately 40 to 42.5 Gy in 15 to 16 fractions, would be appropriate. A boost would be considered based on age, grade, margins, and other risk factors. Because the cancer is left-sided, deep inspiratory breath hold (DIBH) would be considered to reduce cardiac dose.

Still to Decide

Whole breast versus partial breast, whether to add a boost, and how to sequence radiation with endocrine therapy.

The goal is not to recite NCCN from memory. The goal is to be able to say why you think the patient should receive the treatment you're recommending.

Try it yourself: build a one-liner▾

Case: A 64-year-old man with newly diagnosed, locally advanced (T3N1) rectal adenocarcinoma is referred before planned surgery. Pause and draft your own one-liner before reading on.

A strong answer: “This is Mr. K, a 64-year-old man with newly diagnosed, locally advanced T3N1 rectal adenocarcinoma, referred for consideration of neoadjuvant chemoradiation prior to planned surgical resection.”

Worked Example: Full New Patient Oral Presentation

“This is Ms. R, a 58-year-old postmenopausal woman with newly diagnosed, node-negative, ER/PR-positive, HER2-negative invasive ductal carcinoma of the left breast, status post breast-conserving surgery, referred for consideration of adjuvant radiation.

She first noticed a palpable left breast mass on self-exam about six weeks ago. Diagnostic mammogram and ultrasound showed a 1.8-centimeter irregular mass in the upper outer quadrant. Core needle biopsy confirmed grade 2 invasive ductal carcinoma, ER and PR positive and HER2 negative. Two weeks ago, she underwent left lumpectomy with sentinel node biopsy.

On my review of the imaging, I see the index mass in the upper outer quadrant without suspicious contralateral findings or concerning axillary adenopathy. Final surgical pathology showed a 1.7-centimeter invasive ductal carcinoma with negative margins, closest margin 4 millimeters, and 0 of 2 sentinel nodes involved.

I would stage her as pT1c pN0, Stage IA, grade 2, hormone-receptor positive, HER2 negative.

She has no prior breast or chest radiation, no connective tissue disease, and no significant cardiopulmonary disease relevant to left-sided treatment. She is postmenopausal and has already seen medical oncology, who plan adjuvant endocrine therapy.

For assessment and plan, this is adjuvant treatment to reduce local recurrence. My thought is that she's a candidate for either hypofractionated whole-breast radiation or partial-breast irradiation, and does not meet criteria for radiation omission. I'd anticipate a hypofractionated course, with consideration of a boost based on her risk factors, using DIBH because the cancer is left-sided. The plan discussed today is hypofractionated whole-breast radiation with DIBH, which she'd like to proceed with, followed by endocrine therapy.”

The Follow-Up Presentation

A follow-up is fundamentally different from a new consult. You're no longer telling the entire story, you're describing what has changed since the last visit.

What has happened since we last saw this patient?

The Skeleton

  1. One-liner with a time anchor: who they are and how far they are from treatment
  2. Treatment since the last visit
  3. Current disease status: symptoms, exam, and relevant imaging
  4. Toxicity: acute or late, and whether it's improving or worsening
  5. Interval imaging: what was obtained and what it showed
  6. Next step: surveillance, additional workup, or change in management
Worked Example: Follow-Up

“This is Ms. R, now 4 months out from completing adjuvant whole-breast radiation for Stage IA left breast cancer, here for routine follow-up.

Since her last visit, she completed hypofractionated whole-breast radiation without interruption and started her aromatase inhibitor.

She has no new breast symptoms. The surgical site is well healed, and there's no palpable recurrence or adenopathy on exam.

Her acute skin reaction has resolved. She reports mild fatigue that's improving and mild arthralgias after starting the aromatase inhibitor, which she's tolerating.

No interval imaging was indicated today, and she's up to date on surveillance mammography.

The plan is to continue endocrine therapy and routine surveillance with clinical examination and annual mammography, with follow-up in 6 months or sooner for new symptoms.”

The On-Treatment Visit (OTV) Presentation

OTVs are the shortest and most repetitive presentation you'll give. That's exactly why having a consistent structure matters. The purpose is simple: assess how the patient is tolerating treatment and address toxicity before it becomes a problem.

The Skeleton

  1. Current treatment: site, dose, and where they are in the course
  2. Symptoms: overall and site-specific
  3. Toxicity: severity, trajectory, and relevant grading
  4. Focused exam: especially the treatment field and skin
  5. Treatment progress: on track or any interruptions/issues
  6. Plan: continue treatment, adjust supportive care, or make another change
Useful Principle Radiation toxicity accumulates. A patient who feels completely well at fraction 5 may have substantially more symptoms by fraction 20. Many acute toxicities peak toward the end of treatment or shortly afterward, so your job isn't only to document what's happening today, but to anticipate what's coming next.
Worked Example: OTV

“This is Ms. R, on fraction 12 of 15 of hypofractionated whole-breast radiation to the left breast.

Overall, she's doing well and hasn't missed any treatments. Her main complaint is mild fatigue, which has increased over the past week but isn't limiting her activities.

She has grade 1 radiation dermatitis with faint erythema in the treatment field, without moist desquamation. This is stable to slightly progressing, as expected at this point in treatment.

On exam, there's mild pink erythema over the left breast without skin breakdown or signs of infection.

Treatment is proceeding as planned. Plan is to continue treatment, recommend topical emollient and gentle skin care, and counsel her that fatigue and skin changes may continue to increase after treatment before improving.”

High-Yield Summary
  • Do not just relay the chart. Review the imaging, determine the stage, and form your own treatment plan before presenting.
  • New patient: one-liner → chronological history → imaging → pathology → stage → relevant history → assessment → plan.
  • Your plan should have a rationale: know the treatment intent, recommendation, dose/fractionation, technique, and the guideline or trial supporting it.
  • Follow-up: focus on what's changed since the last visit, including treatment, disease status, toxicity, imaging, and next steps.
  • OTV: current treatment → symptoms → toxicity → focused exam → treatment progress → plan.
  • Keep it concise. The goal isn't to prove you know everything in the chart. It's to show you understand the patient and know what matters.

title: The Rad Onc Consult
question: How do I conduct a consultation once I'm in the room?
html:
The consult is where everything starts, and it's one of the places where a well-prepared student can stand out most. This page assumes you've already reviewed the chart and prepared your case presentation (covered in “How to Give a Presentation”). What follows is what happens once you walk into the room: how to talk to the patient, what to ask, and what to pay attention to.

On This Page
  1. Gathering the History
  2. Reviewing the Imaging
  3. Understanding the Patient's Perspective
  4. Know What Your Attending Wants From You
  5. Explaining Radiation: The Spiel

Gathering the History

By the time you enter the room, you should already know most of the patient's oncologic history from the chart. Your job during the encounter is to verify the story, fill in the gaps, and understand the patient's experience of their illness, rather than rediscovering the history from scratch.

Walk the patient through their course and confirm that it matches what you read:

  • How the cancer was diagnosed: presenting symptoms, diagnostic workup, biopsy, and pathology.
  • Prior treatments, in order: surgery, chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and, critically, any prior radiation, including the treatment site and approximate timing. Prior radiation to the same or a nearby area can significantly affect treatment options, so confirm this directly rather than assuming the chart is complete.
  • Anything the chart got wrong or missed: patients often clarify an outside surgery, a treatment that was stopped early, or a date that's incorrect. Reconciling the patient's account with the medical record is an important part of the encounter.

Then bring the history into the present:

  • Current symptoms: pain, bleeding, dysphagia, weight loss, neurologic changes, or anything else related to the current disease. These may themselves become treatment targets or change the urgency of the workup.
  • Focused review of systems: tailor this to the disease site and to symptoms that could affect treatment tolerance or radiation planning. You don't need to perform an exhaustive head-to-toe ROS.

Reviewing the Imaging

After the history, you'll often review the imaging with the patient. Many attendings pull up the scans and show the patient, in plain language, where the cancer is and what area would be treated. Even if you aren't leading this part of the conversation, look at the actual images before the consult, not just the radiology report. You'll follow the attending's discussion more closely, understand the treatment recommendation, and be able to answer questions if they come your way.

Understanding the Patient's Perspective

Before discussing a treatment recommendation, understand how the patient is thinking about their options. Ask what they've been told so far and how they feel about radiation, surgery, chemotherapy, or other treatments. Some patients arrive with a clear preference; others are overwhelmed and haven't yet processed the diagnosis.

Two patients with the same diagnosis may reasonably make different decisions.

Understanding what matters to the patient, and what they already understand, helps the team have a more meaningful treatment discussion.

Know What Your Attending Wants From You

Your role in the consult will depend on the attending and where you are in the rotation:

Scenario 1
Just the HPI

A clean, verified history and the patient's current symptoms, after which the attending will take over the discussion.

Scenario 2
Attempt the Plan

Commit to the stage, treatment intent, and your proposed management, even if you're not sure you're right. Trying to formulate the plan is how you learn.

When in doubt, ask beforehand what they want you to do. Knowing your role prevents both understepping and overstepping.

Explaining Radiation: The “Spiel”

At some point, the patient needs a plain-language explanation of what radiation is and what the treatment process will look like. Most attendings have their own standard “spiel.” Developing your own version is one of the most useful communication skills you can practice during the Sub-I. The goal is to demystify the process, not give a physics lecture.

Sample Script “You're being seen by radiation oncology. We're the doctors who treat cancer using radiation. The radiation itself is a type of x-ray beam, similar to what's used for a CT scan or a regular x-ray. The difference is that we carefully aim the radiation from different directions so the dose is concentrated where we want to treat the cancer.

The process happens in a few steps. First, you'll come in for a simulation, that's a CT scan done in the exact position you'll be treated in, so we can see where the cancer is and plan your treatment accurately. After that, our radiation oncologists, physicists, and dosimetrists build and check your treatment plan. That planning usually takes about one to two weeks.

Then you'll start treatment. You'll come in [Monday through Friday / every other day] for about [X] weeks. You may be here for roughly an hour each visit, although the actual radiation treatment only takes a few minutes, most of that time is spent getting you positioned and lined up correctly. Once treatment is finished, you can go home and continue with your day.

Most people feel relatively well at the beginning of treatment. Side effects tend to build gradually, so the later weeks are often harder than the first few. Fatigue, in particular, can increase as treatment goes on.”

From there, tailor the conversation to the specific side effects expected for that treatment site, such as mucositis and dysphagia for head and neck radiation, skin changes for breast radiation, or bowel and bladder symptoms for pelvic radiation.

A Few Things to Get Right
  • Simulation is not treatment. It's a planning CT performed in the treatment position. Patients often expect treatment to begin that day, so clarify this upfront.
  • The planning interval is intentional. The one to two weeks between simulation and treatment allows the team to contour, develop the plan, review it, and complete quality assurance.
  • Treatment time is mostly setup. Patients often appreciate knowing they may spend about an hour in the department even though the actual radiation delivery is much shorter.
  • Side effects generally build over time. Preparing patients for this helps them recognize expected symptoms and understand why they may feel worse later in the course.
High-Yield Summary
  • Verify rather than rediscover: confirm the oncologic history, prior treatments (especially prior radiation), and current symptoms.
  • Look at the actual imaging: knowing what the cancer looks like on the scan makes the consult much easier to follow.
  • Understand the patient: ask what they know, what they've been told, and what matters to them before discussing treatment.
  • Know your role: clarify whether your attending wants an HPI or a full attempt at the assessment and plan.
  • Have a radiation spiel ready: explain what radiation is, what simulation involves, how planning works, what treatment logistics look like, and how side effects typically evolve.

title: Treatment Planning
question: How do contours and beams actually become a deliverable plan?
html:
Contouring and planning are where a diagnosis on a page becomes an actual, deliverable radiation treatment. Before anything else, hold onto this mental model, because it matters far more than memorizing any acronym:

What are we trying to treat? What margin do we need around it? What do we need to protect nearby? Can we build a plan that covers the target while respecting those normal-tissue limits?

Every contouring and planning decision you'll see on this rotation is, at its core, an attempt to answer those four questions. Everything below is just the vocabulary that goes with each part of the process. Learn the questions first, and the acronyms fall into place.

On This Page
  1. The Framework: CB-CHOP
  2. C — Contours
  3. B — Beams
  4. C — Coverage
  5. H — Hotspots
  6. O — OARs
  7. P — Prescription
  8. Putting It Together

The Framework: CB-CHOP

Here's the good news: you don't have to invent a system for keeping all of this straight. There's a simple checklist, CB-CHOP, that many residents use when they first learn to evaluate a plan. It walks through the same four questions above, in the order you'd actually check them:

C
Contours

Is everything we're treating and protecting drawn correctly?

B
Beams

Does the way we're delivering the radiation make sense?

C
Coverage

Is the target getting its full dose?

H
Hotspots

Are there areas getting more dose than intended?

O
OARs

Are the normal structures within their dose limits?

P
Prescription

Does the plan match what was actually ordered?

The rest of this page walks through each letter and the vocabulary that lives under it. If you learn it this way, you'll be learning it in the exact order an attending runs through a plan on the screen, not as a random pile of terms.

C — Contours: “What Are We Treating, and What Are We Protecting?”

Contouring is drawing, slice by slice, both what you want to treat (target volumes) and what you want to protect (organs at risk). Everything downstream, the beams, the dose, the whole plan, is built on these lines.

Target Volumes: Nested Layers of Margin

Target volumes are drawn as a set of nested structures. Each one starts from the structure inside it and adds a margin for a different kind of uncertainty. Think of them as layers, each answering “what else do I need to cover, given one specific thing I can't be sure about?”

  1. GTV (gross tumor volume): the tumor you can actually see or feel, on imaging or exam. This is your starting point.
  2. CTV (clinical target volume): the GTV plus a margin for microscopic disease that doesn't show up on imaging but is assumed to be there, based on how that cancer type tends to spread.
  3. ITV (internal target volume): the CTV plus a margin for internal organ motion. This matters most for tumors that move when the patient breathes, like lung tumors.
  4. PTV (planning target volume): the outermost layer, adding a margin for daily setup uncertainty, the small, unavoidable variation in how precisely the patient can be positioned each day. This is usually the volume that actually gets prescribed a dose.

The order tells a story: you move outward from the visible tumor (GTV), to where the disease might be hiding (CTV), to how the target moves (ITV), to how reproducibly you can line the patient up each day (PTV).

When a Layer Gets Skipped

Not every case uses every layer. Knowing when a layer is skipped, and why, is exactly the kind of nuance that separates a student who's memorized four letters from one who actually understands the concept.

Vestibular Schwannoma

No CTV. This is a benign, well-circumscribed, non-infiltrative tumor, so there's no meaningful risk of microscopic spread beyond what you can see. GTV goes straight to PTV.

Brain Metastases

No CTV. Same logic as above: mets are sharply marginated on MRI and don't infiltrate microscopically the way a primary malignancy does, so CTV is typically omitted.

Lung Tumor

ITV, via 4D-CT. Because tumors move substantially with respiration, the ITV (sometimes called the iGTV when built directly from the GTV) is captured across every phase of a 4D-CT so the motion envelope is fully covered.

Prostate

No distinct GTV. Prostate cancer is usually microscopic or multifocal within the gland and isn't reliably outlined on standard imaging, so the whole prostate (± seminal vesicles) is contoured directly as the CTV.

B — Beams: “How Are We Delivering It?”

Once the contours exist, look at how the treatment is actually being delivered: the beam or arc arrangement, the energy, and the technique (for example, IMRT or VMAT). The question here is whether the beams make sense for this target and this anatomy, converging on the target while limiting what passes through normal tissue. You don't need to design beams as a Sub-I, but you should be able to look at a plan and see that the beams are aimed to build dose up at the target and spread the unavoidable dose across normal tissue rather than dumping it all in one place.

C — Coverage: “Is the Target Getting Its Full Dose?”

Coverage asks whether the target volume is receiving the prescribed dose throughout its entirety, not just in the center. The edges of the PTV are the easy place to fall short, so this is where you confirm the whole target, borders included, is getting what it's supposed to.

A closely related term is conformity: how tightly the high-dose region hugs the shape of the target rather than spilling into surrounding normal tissue. Coverage and conformity are two sides of the same coin: coverage asks “is the target getting enough?” and conformity asks “is everything else being spared?” Both are read off the dose distribution, the way dose is spread across the treated area, usually shown with isodose lines (see “How Radiation Works”).

H — Hotspots: “Is Anywhere Getting Too Much?”

Hotspots are small areas within or near the target getting a higher dose than intended. Some degree of hotspot is often unavoidable and acceptable. What you're checking for is whether a hotspot is large, or sitting somewhere it shouldn't, especially inside an OAR, where a small area of excess dose can cause real harm. A hotspot in the middle of the tumor is usually fine; a hotspot in the spinal cord is not.

O — OARs: “Are the Normal Structures Within Their Limits?”

You contoured the OARs back in the first step; now you check their dose. This is where the DVH (dose-volume histogram) does the heavy lifting. The DVH is a graph, used constantly in plan review, that shows what percentage of a structure's volume is receiving at least a given dose. Instead of scrolling through every CT slice, a physician can glance at the DVH and ask, “is too much of the parotid getting too much dose?”

Organs at Risk: What You're Drawing to Protect

The other half of contouring is the organs at risk (OARs), the normal structures near the target that could be damaged by radiation. These get contoured too, because radiation doesn't tell tumor and normal tissue apart on its own. If a structure isn't drawn, the plan can't be steered around it, so the contour is the first step in protecting it.

Which OARs matter depends entirely on where the tumor is. A good way to build intuition is head and neck cancer, one of the most anatomically crowded, OAR-dense sites you'll see. Common OARs there include:

  • Spinal cord and brainstem: serial structures where a single small hotspot can matter, so the maximum dose is what you watch. These have hard limits because the consequence of exceeding them (myelopathy) is catastrophic and permanent.
  • Parotid glands: sparing these helps prevent permanent dry mouth (xerostomia), one of the most quality-of-life-limiting late effects in head and neck treatment. Here the mean dose to the gland is what matters most.
  • Mandible: high dose raises the risk of osteoradionecrosis.
  • Larynx: protected when it isn't itself the target, to limit voice and swallowing toxicity.

Notice the pattern worth carrying to every site: some OARs are judged by their maximum dose (a “don't exceed this single point” structure, like spinal cord) and others by their mean dose or by how much volume gets a certain dose (like the parotid or lung). That distinction drives how the plan is shaped and how you'll read the DVH later. Every disease site has its own characteristic set of OARs and its own version of these rules, which you'll pick up in the disease-site modules.

P — Prescription: “Does the Plan Match the Order?”

The last check is the simplest, and easy to take for granted: confirm the plan matches the intended prescription, the right total dose, dose per fraction, number of fractions, and target. It sounds obvious, but it's the final safety check before a plan moves forward, and it's exactly the kind of thing a checklist exists to catch.

Putting It Together

When you watch an attending review a plan, what looks like a fast, intuitive glance is really CB-CHOP running in their head: are the contours right, do the beams make sense, is the target covered, are there any bad hotspots, are the OARs within limits on the DVH, and does it all match the prescription. If you follow along with that same checklist during plan review, you'll get far more out of those sessions than if you're trying to remember what each acronym stands for in the moment.

High-Yield Summary
  • The mental model that matters most: what are we treating, what margin does it need, what do we need to protect, and can we build a plan that does both?
  • CB-CHOP is the checklist that ties it all together: Contours, Beams, Coverage, Hotspots, OARs, Prescription.
  • Target volumes nest outward: GTV (visible tumor) → CTV (adds a margin for microscopic disease) → ITV (adds a margin for internal motion) → PTV (adds a margin for daily setup uncertainty). Not every case uses every layer.
  • OARs are the normal structures you contour to protect; they're judged by maximum, mean, or volume-based constraints depending on the organ, and every disease site has its own set.
  • The DVH is the graph you'll use constantly to check each OAR against its constraint.
  • Coverage vs. conformity: coverage asks whether the target gets its dose; conformity asks whether everything else is spared. Balancing the two against OAR limits is the core of plan review.
